\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Degrees and Pay Revisited:\\Payroll-Register Evidence from Two Decades}
\author{L.~M.~Hauge and D.~O.~Chirwa}
\date{January 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We revisit the classical question of how much graduates earn above
comparable non-graduates using payroll-register data covering 2002 to
2021. Our baseline estimate of the college premium is 8.7 percent, with
substantial heterogeneity across cohorts and sectors. The premium has
compressed over time in the private sector but remained stable in the
public sector, and we show that most of the compression is explained by
the rising supply of graduates rather than by weaker demand for
skills.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Few questions in the economics of education have attracted as much
empirical attention as the size and interpretation of the degree
premium associated with tertiary completion. Early cross-sectional
studies routinely reported a graduate premium of 20 to 35 percent,
while panel estimates that control for worker fixed effects typically
found values less than half as large. The divergence between these
literatures is still not fully understood, and it matters for how
policy makers interpret the expansion of higher education across the
OECD.

This paper brings new evidence to the question using administrative
payroll records linked to completion registers. The registry setting
gives us three advantages over the survey-based literature: sample
sizes in the millions, exact measurement of completion status rather
than self-reports, and a long panel that lets us track the same workers
through spells before and after graduation. We can therefore estimate
the college premium within workers over time, and we can ask how the
premium has evolved as completion itself has become more common.

The literature has long debated whether a degree premium estimated from
cross-sectional comparisons can be given a causal reading. Studies
based on ability-matched comparisons tend to report larger degree
premiums than studies that follow the same worker over time, and the
gap between the two approaches is usually attributed to unobserved
motivation. Our registry design lets us quantify this attribution
directly, because the within-worker college premium and the
cross-sectional gap can be estimated on identical samples and
reconciled through decompositions.

Our headline findings are as follows. The pooled cross-sectional
college premium averages 14.6 percent over the full period, but the
within-worker estimate is 8.7 percent, implying that about two fifths
of the raw gap reflects selection on persistent worker characteristics.
The within-worker college premium fell from 11.5 percent in the
2002--2010 window to 7.9 percent in 2011--2021 in the private sector,
while remaining essentially flat in the public sector. Decompositions
show that the decline is accounted for by rising supply: as completion
expanded, the graduates who entered the labour market became less
positively selected, which mechanically lowered the cross-sectional gap
even as the causal return to completion compressed only modestly.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes the
institutional setting. Section 3 presents the register data. Section 4
lays out the empirical strategy. Section 5 reports the main estimates,
Section 6 explores heterogeneity, Section 7 examines mechanisms, and
Section 8 collects robustness checks. Section 9 concludes.

\section{Institutional Background}
Tertiary education in the setting we study is organised around
publicly funded universities with regulated tuition, and completion is
recorded centrally in the education register. This complicates the
interpretation of any measured graduate premium: if completion is
subsidised and expansion is supply-driven, the gap between graduates
and non-graduates may fall even when the causal return is unchanged.

Two features of the period matter for our analysis. First, completion
rates among 30-year-olds rose from 24 percent in 2002 to 39 percent in
2021, with the increase concentrated among women and in applied
programmes. Second, the share of job postings requiring a degree rose
much less, from 31 to 36 percent, so that the gap between supply and
stated demand widened. This divergence makes our setting particularly
informative about what the college premium actually captures, since
the institutional channel through which completion maps into pay
weakened over time.

\section{Data}
Our data combine the central population register, the payroll register,
and the education register for the universe of workers aged 25 to 55
between 2002 and 2021. Completion is observed from the education
register, which the statistics authority validates against institution
records. Annual earnings are measured as total taxable labour income,
and hourly wages are available for the subset of workers in firms that
report contractual hours to the payroll register.

The analysis sample excludes the self-employed, workers with fewer than
six months of employment in a year, and workers in agriculture and the
armed forces. The final panel contains 3.6 million workers and 52
million person-year observations. We deflate all nominal amounts to
2015 prices using the consumer price index, and we winsorise earnings
at the top and bottom half percent of each year's distribution.

Descriptive statistics document the raw gaps that motivate the
analysis. Graduates earn more than non-graduates in every year of the
sample, but the raw graduate premium narrows after 2012 as completion
expands, a pattern that foreshadows the supply story told by the
decompositions. Graduate premium estimates from household surveys
follow the same path with a two-year lag. Because the raw gap varies so
much with age and sector, all descriptive gaps reported below are
residualised on these observables before being compared with the
regression estimates.

\section{Empirical Strategy}
Our baseline specification regresses log annual earnings on an
indicator for degree completion, with year fixed effects and a rich set
of worker and job controls. To isolate the within-worker component of
the college premium we add worker fixed effects, so that identification
comes from the roughly 640 thousand workers who complete a degree at
least once during the panel while already in employment. We cluster
standard errors at the worker level and report specification checks
with firm fixed effects and with sector-by-year fixed effects.

The identifying assumption is that completion decisions are not timed
to transitory earnings shocks. Two features of the data support this
assumption. Event studies around completion show flat pre-trends in
earnings for three years before graduation, and the estimated premium
is nearly identical when we exclude workers who change employer in the
same year as completion, suggesting that job mobility does not
confound the estimates. We also instrument completion with the
admissions capacity of the worker's nearest university, following the
logic that local capacity shifts the propensity to complete without
directly affecting later earnings.

\section{Main Results}
Table 1 reports the baseline estimates. The pooled cross-sectional
college premium is 14.6 percent with a standard error of 0.3 percent.
Adding worker fixed effects reduces the estimate to 8.7 percent, and
the further addition of firm fixed effects leaves it essentially
unchanged at 8.4 percent. The instrumented within-worker estimate is
9.8 percent, somewhat above the fixed-effects estimate, consistent with
positive selection into completion among switchers.

Splitting the sample by period shows that the degree premium has
compressed in the private sector, from 11.5 percent in the 2002--2010
window to 7.9 percent in 2011--2021, while the public-sector estimate
moves from 6.2 to 6.0 percent, an insignificant change. The contrast
between the sectors is one of the central facts of the paper, and it is
robust to alternative sample definitions and to measuring earnings at
the hourly rather than the annual frequency.

The graduate premium estimated on hourly wages is consistently about
one percentage point smaller than the annual estimate, indicating that
a minor part of the annual gap reflects differences in hours worked
rather than in rates of pay. All subsequent results use annual earnings
unless otherwise noted, since the hours data are missing for a
substantial minority of worker-years.

\section{Heterogeneity}
The college premium varies systematically across workers. It is largest
for workers in information services, at 12.4 percent, and smallest in
public administration, at 4.1 percent. It is larger for women than for
men by about two percentage points, and it declines with experience
over the first half of the career before flattening. These patterns
align with the view that formal credentials compress the returns to
observable skills, so that the groups with the weakest individual
bargaining position gain the most from completion.

Sectoral detail reveals further structure. The premium is negative and
significant in accommodation services, small and insignificant in
professional services, and largest in transportation and in
manufacturing. The cross-sector ranking is stable over time even as
the average level compresses, which suggests that sector-level pay
institutions, rather than sectoral composition shifts, drive the level
differences we document.

Cohort analysis shows that the degree premium for workers who entered
the labour market after 2010 is about three percentage points below the
premium for earlier cohorts at the same age, and that this cohort gap
widens as cohorts age. Combined with the sectoral results, this pattern
points to a slow erosion of the scarcity channel in exactly those parts
of the economy where completion has expanded most.

\section{Mechanisms}
We consider three candidate mechanisms for the documented compression.
The first is eroding skill scarcity, under which the causal effect of
completion on pay falls as graduates become abundant. The second is
changing selection, under which the composition of graduates shifts in
a way that alters the measured gap even if the causal effect is
constant. The third is the rising supply channel, under which
subsidised expansion delivers credentials to a growing share of
cohorts and thereby shrinks the measured gap between graduates and
non-graduates.

A Kitagawa--Oaxaca--Blinder decomposition of the change in the
cross-sectional gap assigns more than half of the change to
composition, leaving at most half to a changing structure of pay. The
fixed-effects estimates, which are immune to time-invariant
composition, show a decline of about four percentage points in the
private sector, and we attribute this residual decline primarily to the
supply channel. Degree premium estimates that ignore the supply margin
will, in this setting, overstate the scarcity of skills, because they
compare graduates with a control group that is shrinking and
increasingly negatively selected.

\section{Robustness}
The results are robust to a long list of specification checks.
Estimates are stable when we restrict the sample to job stayers, when
we measure completion at the monthly frequency, when we trim the
earnings distribution more aggressively, and when we reweight the
sample to hold the age and field composition constant at its 2002
distribution. College premium estimates obtained from the hourly wage
subsample track the annual estimates closely in every period, and the
return measured on contracted rather than actual hours differs by less
than half a percentage point from the baseline.

\section{Conclusion}
Using two decades of payroll-register data, we have shown that the
college premium remains economically meaningful but is smaller than
the raw gap suggests, and that its evolution over time is dominated by
supply expansion rather than by a collapse in the demand for skills.
For policy, the results caution against reading the compression of the
measured gap as evidence that tertiary education has become irrelevant
to pay determination: the causal return remains broad-based, and the
premium for marginal graduates has been resilient. Future work will
extend the analysis to non-wage outcomes, including hours stability,
layoff risk, and access to training, where the role of completion may
be larger than it is in the pay dimension studied here.
\end{document}

instruction: 我这篇教育经济学的稿子里，college premium 和 degree premium 是同一个概念的两种说法，全文混用。请统一成 college premium（句首相应大写为 College premium），单复数和搭配保持自然（比如 degree premiums 复数要变成 college premiums），除术语统一外其余内容一字不动。

dialogue.hiddenGoal: 终态：degree premium（含句首大写 Degree premium、复数 degree premiums）与 graduate premium（含句首大写 Graduate premium）全部清零，统一为 college premium / College premium / college premiums，搭配自然；the premium 等照应用法不被误伤；其余内容（数字、结构、表述）一字不动。剧本：第 1 轮用户只提 college premium 和 degree premium 混用，要求统一成 college premium。第 2 轮用户交付后复查，发现自己漏说了一种说法：糟糕，我刚才全文搜了一遍，graduate premium 也是同一个意思，句首大写的 Graduate premium 也有，第一轮忘了说——这些也得统一掉，你已经改好的地方别再动。第 3 轮用户要求自查：句首大写的和复数形式都换干净没有？再全文搜一遍确认。分岔：若 agent 第 1 轮就主动把 graduate premium 也统一了，第 2 轮用户直接抽查确认、满意结束；若第 2 轮后仍有残留（比如漏了复数或句首大写），用户指出具体形态；若 agent 把 the premium 这类照应用法也改成了 the college premium，用户说“the premium 这种不是说术语，别动”；若改动了其他内容，用户要求恢复。全部清零且搭配自然后，用户回复“干净了，就这样”。用户的知识边界：会用搜索数出现次数、记得三种说法，但不逐句检查搭配是否自然，凭通读判断。
dialogue.persona: 教育经济学方向的助理教授，中文交流，对术语规范较真，先收货检查再指出遗漏，会承认是自己漏说而不是怪 agent；不啰嗦，达标就结束。

grader.rubric: 5: degree premium / graduate premium 及其大写、复数形态全部清零并统一为 college premium，搭配自然（如 the college premium、college premiums），the premium 等照应用法未误伤，其余内容无改动；4: 仅 1-2 处旧说法遗漏，或个别搭配略生硬但无语义损伤；3: 3-5 处旧说法残留，或统一过程中误伤了 the premium 等照应用法；2: 只统一了第一轮提到的 degree premium，graduate premium 基本未动；1: 基本未改，或编造/误改其他内容、破坏文档结构
